title: Egushawa and the Odawa in Kentucky’s War Years
summary: Odawa war chief Egushawa helped Britain recruit allies against Kentucky and led Ottawa warriors in the 1780 capture of Ruddell’s and Martin’s stations.
bodyMarkdown:
[Egushawa](/people/#egushawa), also written Au-goosh-away, was an Odawa war chief from the Detroit country. Some writers call him Pontiac's successor. His people, the [Odawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa), lived around the upper Great Lakes and traded at Detroit. They did not live in Kentucky, but in the Revolution their warriors came south.

British officers at Detroit wanted allies against the Kentucky stations. Egushawa helped them recruit Odawa, Wabash, and other Great Lakes warriors. He had weight in the councils, and the British leaned on it.

In the spring of 1780 Capt. [Henry Bird](/people/#henry-bird) led a force south from Detroit: British soldiers, Canadian militia, and hundreds of warriors from several nations. Egushawa led an Odawa contingent. Unlike most war parties, this one brought cannon.

In June the force reached [Ruddell's Station](/stories/isaac-ruddell-and-the-guns-at-ruddells-station/) in what is now Harrison County. Log walls could not stand up to cannon, and [Isaac Ruddell](/people/#isaac-ruddell) surrendered. Martin's Station fell next. Bird marched hundreds of prisoners, men, women, and children, north toward Detroit. Some were killed on the way. Others lived for years in Native towns or in Canada before coming home. The raid came down past the forks at [Falmouth](/stories/falmouth-at-the-licking-forks/), and [Lenape warriors](/stories/delaware-lenape-in-the-1780-kentucky-raids/) and [Ojibwe](/stories/ojibwe-on-birds-war-road/) were in it too.

The Revolution ended in 1783, but Egushawa's war did not. He said land cessions made without the consent of the nations were worthless. He joined the Northwest Confederacy led by [Blue Jacket](/stories/blue-jacket-weyapiersenwah/) and [Little Turtle](/people/#little-turtle), and Odawa warriors fought in the victories over Josiah Harmar in 1790 and Arthur St. Clair in 1791.

At Fallen Timbers in 1794 Egushawa was badly wounded. The next year he signed the [Treaty of Greenville](/stories/treaty-of-greenville-1795-the-line-to-the-kentucky-river/) as a leading Odawa speaker. He died a few years later. His life ties the Odawa towns near Detroit to the raids that shaped Kentucky's last Revolutionary years.

## Kentucky today

No Odawa town stood in Kentucky. The 1780 raid is remembered in Harrison and Bourbon counties, where state historical markers tell the story of Ruddell's and Martin's stations.
